standard: Detailed exam explanations: context, key people, sequence, causes, significance, exam memory hook and source link.

31.title: The Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro
31.overview: The Great Bath is a large, carefully built water tank at Mohenjo-daro, one of the major cities of the Indus Valley Civilisation (Harappan Civilisation).
31.context: Mohenjo-daro flourished in the mature Harappan phase, roughly 2600–1900 BCE, in the Indus river system. Its planned streets, drainage, wells and public buildings show organised urban life.
31.who: No individual builder is known. Archaeologists identify the structure from excavations; its precise religious or civic purpose remains debated.
31.what: The tank was built with baked bricks, a waterproof lining and steps leading down at both ends. Rooms and a well nearby may have supported filling and changing, but the exact use is not proven.
31.why: Its careful waterproof construction suggests that water had an important communal or possibly ritual role. Calling it a bathing tank is a widely used interpretation, not a certainty about every activity performed there.
31.significance: It is evidence of Harappan engineering, brick technology, water management and public architecture.
31.exam: Mohenjo-daro = Great Bath. Do not confuse it with Lothal's dockyard or the granary-like structures at other Harappan sites.

32.title: Buddhism: the Four Noble Truths
32.overview: The Four Noble Truths are the central framework in the Buddha's first teaching: suffering exists; it has causes; it can end; and there is a path leading to its end.
32.context: Siddhartha Gautama, later known as the Buddha, taught in north India around the 6th–5th century BCE. Buddhist traditions describe his first sermon at Sarnath after enlightenment.
32.who: The teaching is attributed to Gautama Buddha; it was transmitted by his followers and preserved in Buddhist traditions.
32.what: The truths are: (1) dukkha—life involves suffering or unsatisfactoriness; (2) samudaya—craving and attachment cause it; (3) nirodha—cessation is possible; (4) magga—the Noble Eightfold Path leads to cessation.
32.why: The teaching explains both the problem and a practical route to liberation, rather than simply describing suffering.
32.significance: It is foundational to Buddhist doctrine and connects directly with the Middle Way and the Noble Eightfold Path.
32.exam: Four Noble Truths = Buddhism; Eightfold Path = practical path; avoid attributing them to Jainism.

33.title: Chandragupta Maurya and the Mauryan Empire
33.overview: Chandragupta Maurya established the Mauryan Empire in the late 4th century BCE, creating a large state centred on Magadha with its capital at Pataliputra.
33.context: After the campaigns of Alexander in the north-west and amid competing mahajanapadas and the Nanda power in Magadha, a new imperial state emerged.
33.who: Chandragupta Maurya was the founder. Chanakya (also known as Kautilya or Vishnugupta) is traditionally associated with advising him. Bindusara succeeded Chandragupta; Ashoka was a later Mauryan ruler, not the founder.
33.what: Chandragupta defeated the Nanda dynasty according to later accounts, consolidated Magadha and expanded Mauryan control across much of the subcontinent. He also made an agreement with Seleucus I Nicator after conflict in the north-west.
33.why: A strong central administration, military organisation and control of strategic routes helped the new empire consolidate power.
33.significance: The Mauryan state became one of the largest early empires in South Asian history. The Arthashastra is traditionally associated with Kautilya, though its composition history is complex.
33.exam: Founder = Chandragupta Maurya; successor = Bindusara; famous grandson = Ashoka.

34.title: Battle of Plassey, 23 June 1757
34.overview: The Battle of Plassey was fought in Bengal on 23 June 1757 between the East India Company forces led by Robert Clive and the army of Nawab Siraj-ud-Daulah.
34.context: The Company and the Nawab were in conflict over the Company's fortifications, trade privileges and political interference in Bengal. The capture of Calcutta and the 1756 events intensified the dispute.
34.who: Robert Clive commanded the Company force. Siraj-ud-Daulah was the Nawab of Bengal. Mir Jafar, a senior commander, entered into a secret understanding with the Company and did not effectively support the Nawab during the battle.
34.what: The Company force defeated Siraj-ud-Daulah's army after key sections under Mir Jafar withheld support. Siraj was later captured and killed. Mir Jafar was installed as Nawab under Company influence.
34.why: The Company sought secure commercial privileges and political leverage; local court rivalries and the conspiracy around Mir Jafar shaped the outcome.
34.significance: Plassey marked a major step in the East India Company's political control in Bengal. The Company gained decisive influence, followed by further expansion and the acquisition of revenue rights after Buxar and the 1765 Diwani grant.
34.exam: Plassey = 1757; Buxar = 1764. Robert Clive led the Company side; Siraj-ud-Daulah was the Nawab.

35.title: Jallianwala Bagh massacre, 13 April 1919
35.overview: On 13 April 1919, troops commanded by Brigadier-General Reginald Edward Harry Dyer opened fire on a large gathering of unarmed people at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar, Punjab. Hundreds were killed and many more wounded.
35.context: The Rowlatt Act of 1919 extended extraordinary powers of detention and restrictions without ordinary trial safeguards, prompting protests. In Amritsar, popular anger intensified after the arrest and deportation of local leaders Dr Saifuddin Kitchlew and Dr Satyapal. 13 April was Baisakhi, when visitors from nearby areas also came to the city.
35.who: Reginald Dyer commanded the troops and ordered the firing. The crowd included people attending a meeting and Baisakhi visitors; it was not a group of armed combatants. Sir Michael O'Dwyer was the Lieutenant-Governor of Punjab at the time—he was a different person from General Dyer.
35.what: Dyer entered the enclosed garden with troops and ordered them to fire without first giving the crowd a warning to disperse. The troops fired for about ten minutes; the narrow exits and surrounding buildings made escape difficult. Some people tried to flee through the gates and some jumped into the well.
35.why: The colonial authorities were trying to suppress unrest and defiance of restrictions in Punjab. Dyer later defended the firing as an attempt to produce a wider deterrent effect; that was his stated justification, not a justification for the killing of civilians.
35.significance: The official Hunter Committee figure was 379 dead; the number of wounded was estimated at around three times that figure. Other estimates of deaths are higher, so exam answers should identify 379 as the official inquiry figure and note that totals are disputed. The massacre intensified opposition to British rule. Rabindranath Tagore renounced his knighthood, and Gandhi's trust in the justice of British rule was deeply shaken.
35.exam: Date = 13 April 1919; place = Amritsar; commander who ordered firing = Reginald Dyer; official Hunter Committee death figure = 379. Do not confuse General Dyer with Lieutenant-Governor Michael O'Dwyer.
35.source: UK Parliament: Hunter Commission records; PIB historical account

36.title: Dandi March and the Salt Satyagraha, 1930
36.overview: The Dandi March was a 24-day march led by Mahatma Gandhi from Sabarmati Ashram to the coastal village of Dandi in Gujarat, where he broke the British salt law on 6 April 1930.
36.context: The colonial government controlled salt production and imposed a tax. Salt was a daily necessity used by rich and poor, making the law a powerful symbol of colonial economic control.
36.who: Gandhi led the march, beginning with 78 selected volunteers on 12 March 1930. Thousands joined or supported the wider campaign along the route and across India.
36.what: After walking roughly 390 km, Gandhi picked up natural salt at Dandi, openly defying the law. The act inspired people in many regions to make or sell salt illegally and to join wider civil disobedience.
36.why: Gandhi chose salt because the tax affected ordinary households and offered a simple, visible way to challenge colonial authority through non-violent action.
36.significance: The Salt Satyagraha became the opening action of the Civil Disobedience Movement and drew national and international attention.
36.exam: March began 12 March 1930; salt law broken at Dandi on 6 April 1930; leader = Mahatma Gandhi.

37.title: Quit India Movement, August 1942
37.overview: The Quit India Movement was launched by the Indian National Congress in August 1942, demanding an end to British rule in India during the Second World War.
37.context: The failure of the Cripps Mission, wartime pressures and the refusal to transfer meaningful power increased frustration among Indian nationalists.
37.who: The Congress Working Committee adopted the resolution at Bombay on 8 August 1942. Mahatma Gandhi gave the call for the British to leave India. Senior leaders, including Gandhi, Nehru, Patel and others, were arrested soon after the launch.
37.what: Mass protests, strikes, demonstrations and acts of civil resistance spread. With national leaders imprisoned, local and underground networks continued activity. Some areas saw sabotage and parallel local administrations; the movement was not uniform everywhere.
37.why: Nationalists argued that India should not be compelled to support a world war while denied freedom and self-government.
37.significance: Although suppressed by the colonial government, the movement demonstrated the depth of opposition to British rule and became a major final phase in the freedom struggle before independence in 1947.
37.exam: Year = 1942; resolution = Bombay, 8 August; slogan = Do or Die; leader most associated with the call = Mahatma Gandhi.

38.title: The slogan 'Do or Die'
38.overview: Mahatma Gandhi used the call 'Do or Die' during the launch of the Quit India Movement in August 1942.
38.context: The call came after the failure of the Cripps Mission and the Congress demand for an immediate end to British rule during World War II.
38.who: Mahatma Gandhi delivered the call to the people and delegates at the All-India Congress Committee meeting in Bombay.
38.what: It urged people to commit themselves to achieving freedom through determined non-violent struggle, rather than accept continued colonial rule.
38.why: Gandhi wanted to communicate urgency and total commitment at a moment when the national movement was demanding immediate independence.
38.significance: The phrase became closely associated with the Quit India Movement and the final mass phase of the freedom struggle.
38.exam: 'Do or Die' = Gandhi = Quit India Movement = 1942.

39.title: Cabinet Mission, 1946
39.overview: The Cabinet Mission was a three-member British delegation sent to India in 1946 to discuss the transfer of power and a constitutional framework for an independent India.
39.context: After World War II, the British government announced that it intended to transfer power. Congress and the Muslim League disagreed over the shape of India's future constitution and the demand for Pakistan.
39.who: The mission consisted of Lord Pethick-Lawrence, Sir Stafford Cripps and A.V. Alexander.
39.what: It proposed a Union dealing mainly with foreign affairs, defence and communications, with provinces grouped into sections and a Constituent Assembly to frame the constitution. The plan did not resolve the political deadlock.
39.why: Britain sought an agreed constitutional process for transferring power while attempting to keep India united.
39.significance: The plan led to the formation of the Constituent Assembly process, although disagreement and political conflict continued and partition followed in 1947.
39.exam: Cabinet Mission = 1946; members = Pethick-Lawrence, Stafford Cripps and A.V. Alexander.

40.title: The Discovery of India
40.overview: The Discovery of India is a historical and cultural reflection on India written by Jawaharlal Nehru while imprisoned at Ahmednagar Fort during 1942–1945.
40.context: Nehru wrote the book during the period of his detention following the Quit India Movement. It explores India's long history, civilisation, religions, society and the development of its national identity.
40.what: The book moves across ancient, medieval and modern Indian history and considers how different traditions and communities contributed to Indian civilisation.
40.why: Nehru sought to understand India's historical continuity and diversity at a time when the freedom struggle was approaching its final phase.
40.significance: It is an important work of modern Indian political and historical writing, often used to understand Nehru's interpretation of Indian civilisation.
40.exam: Author = Jawaharlal Nehru; written largely during imprisonment at Ahmednagar Fort, 1942–1945.

110.title: Buddhism: the Four Noble Truths
110.overview: The Four Noble Truths are the central framework in the Buddha's first teaching: suffering exists; it has causes; it can end; and there is a path leading to its end.
110.context: Siddhartha Gautama, later known as the Buddha, taught in north India around the 6th–5th century BCE. Buddhist traditions describe his first sermon at Sarnath after enlightenment.
110.who: The teaching is attributed to Gautama Buddha; it was transmitted by his followers and preserved in Buddhist traditions.
110.what: The truths are: (1) dukkha—life involves suffering or unsatisfactoriness; (2) samudaya—craving and attachment cause it; (3) nirodha—cessation is possible; (4) magga—the Noble Eightfold Path leads to cessation.
110.why: The teaching explains both the problem and a practical route to liberation, rather than simply describing suffering.
110.significance: It is foundational to Buddhist doctrine and connects directly with the Middle Way and the Noble Eightfold Path.
110.exam: Four Noble Truths = Buddhism; Eightfold Path = practical path; avoid attributing them to Jainism.

112.title: George Orwell and the novel 1984
112.overview: Nineteen Eighty-Four (1984) is a dystopian novel by the English writer George Orwell, published in 1949.
112.context: The novel imagines a totalitarian state that uses surveillance, propaganda, censorship and control of language to dominate citizens.
112.who: George Orwell, whose real name was Eric Arthur Blair, wrote the novel.
112.what: The story follows Winston Smith, who works in the state's Records Department and begins to question the Party's control over truth and private life.
112.why: Orwell explored the dangers of authoritarian power, political manipulation and the destruction of independent thought.
112.significance: The novel popularised terms and ideas such as Big Brother and thoughtcrime in discussions of surveillance and authoritarianism.
112.exam: 1984 = George Orwell; Animal Farm is also by Orwell. Do not confuse 1984 with Aldous Huxley's Brave New World.

146.title: Non-Cooperation Movement, 1920–1922
146.overview: The Non-Cooperation Movement was a mass campaign led by Gandhi and the Indian National Congress to withdraw cooperation from British institutions and authority.
146.context: It followed the Rowlatt agitation and the Jallianwala Bagh massacre. The Khilafat issue also brought many Indian Muslims into a shared anti-colonial mobilisation.
146.who: Mahatma Gandhi became its leading figure; the Congress adopted the programme in 1920. Many students, lawyers, workers, peasants and traders participated in different regions.
146.what: Participants boycotted government schools and colleges, law courts, legislatures, foreign cloth and titles. Promotion of khadi and national institutions formed part of the constructive programme.
146.why: The strategy aimed to weaken colonial rule by withdrawing voluntary cooperation without resorting to armed revolt.
146.significance: The movement made nationalism a mass political force. Gandhi suspended it in February 1922 after the violent Chauri Chaura incident.
146.exam: Launched 1920; withdrawn 1922 after Chauri Chaura; do not confuse with Civil Disobedience (1930) or Quit India (1942).

147.title: Rowlatt Act, 1919
147.overview: The Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act of 1919, commonly called the Rowlatt Act, extended emergency powers that allowed detention and special trials with limited safeguards.
147.context: The British government argued that revolutionary activity continued after World War I and sought powers to suppress it, despite wartime emergency conditions having ended.
147.who: The legislation followed recommendations of the Rowlatt Committee, chaired by Justice Sidney Rowlatt. Indian political leaders across different groups opposed it.
147.what: The Act enabled detention without ordinary trial safeguards and restrictions on political activity. Gandhi called for a nationwide satyagraha against it.
147.why: The colonial government sought to control revolutionary and nationalist activity; Indian critics saw the law as a denial of civil liberties and justice.
147.significance: The protests contributed to the nationwide agitation of 1919 and form essential background to the events in Punjab, including the Jallianwala Bagh massacre.
147.exam: Rowlatt Act = 1919; committee chairman = Sidney Rowlatt; common description = 'Black Act'.

148.title: Government of India Act, 1935
148.overview: The Government of India Act, 1935 was a major constitutional statute that proposed an all-India federation and introduced provincial autonomy.
148.context: It followed constitutional negotiations, the Simon Commission, Round Table Conferences and the 1933 White Paper.
148.who: The Act was passed by the British Parliament; it was not an Indian constitution adopted by a sovereign assembly.
148.what: Provincial dyarchy was abolished and provincial autonomy introduced. The Act proposed a federation, but that part did not come into operation. It also provided for a Federal Court, established in 1937.
148.why: The British government sought to restructure colonial administration while retaining substantial imperial control.
148.significance: It shaped provincial politics and influenced parts of the later constitutional framework, but it did not grant independence or universal adult franchise.
148.exam: 1935 Act = provincial autonomy; provincial elections held in 1937; proposed federation never fully came into operation.

149.title: Lucknow Pact, 1916
149.overview: The Lucknow Pact was an agreement reached in 1916 between the Indian National Congress and the All-India Muslim League on constitutional demands and political representation.
149.context: Nationalist leaders were seeking constitutional reforms and greater Indian participation in government. The Congress also saw a reunion of its moderate and extremist factions at Lucknow in 1916.
149.who: Congress and the Muslim League leaders negotiated the agreement; prominent figures included Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Muhammad Ali Jinnah in the wider political developments of the period.
149.what: The organisations agreed on a set of constitutional demands, including elected majorities in legislative councils and separate electorates for Muslims, with specified representation.
149.why: The pact aimed to present a united political demand to the British government and strengthen pressure for constitutional reform.
149.significance: It marked a notable moment of Congress–League cooperation, though the separate-electorate arrangement had long-term political implications.
149.exam: Lucknow Pact = 1916; Congress–Muslim League agreement; separate electorates were part of the arrangement.

150.title: Civil Disobedience Movement
150.overview: The Civil Disobedience Movement began in 1930 with Gandhi's Salt March and the deliberate violation of the British salt law.
150.context: After the Congress declared Purna Swaraj (complete independence) at the Lahore session in December 1929, 26 January 1930 was observed as Independence Day. Gandhi then selected salt as the first issue for mass action.
150.who: Mahatma Gandhi led the Dandi March; Congress leaders and ordinary people across India participated in civil disobedience campaigns.
150.what: People broke salt laws, refused certain taxes, boycotted foreign goods and challenged colonial regulations in different regions. The forms of protest varied by locality.
150.why: The movement aimed to make the demand for complete independence practical and visible through peaceful defiance of unjust colonial laws.
150.significance: It widened mass participation and led to negotiations including the Gandhi–Irwin Pact of 1931, though the struggle later resumed.
150.exam: Civil Disobedience = 1930; launched with Salt March; Purna Swaraj resolution = Lahore session, 1929.

211.title: Rig Veda
211.overview: The Rig Veda is the oldest of the four Vedas and is primarily a collection of hymns composed in Vedic Sanskrit.
211.context: Its hymns belong to the early Vedic tradition and provide evidence about religious practices, social life, nature and ideas of early Indo-Aryan communities.
211.who: The hymns are attributed in the tradition to different rishis and families of composers; it is not the work of a single author.
211.what: The text contains ten mandalas and hymns addressed to deities such as Agni, Indra and Soma.
211.why: The hymns were used in ritual and oral transmission, preserving religious poetry and knowledge across generations.
211.significance: It is a key source for the study of early Vedic society, religion and language.
211.exam: Rig Veda = hymns; four Vedas = Rig, Sama, Yajur and Atharva.

212.title: Upanishads
212.overview: The Upanishads are philosophical texts associated with the later Vedic tradition and explore questions about the self, ultimate reality, knowledge and liberation.
212.context: They developed over a long period and form part of the concluding portions of Vedic literature, which is why they are also called Vedanta.
212.who: Different Upanishads are associated with different teachers and schools; there is no single author for the entire corpus.
212.what: Many Upanishads discuss concepts such as Brahman (ultimate reality), Atman (self), knowledge and the relationship between them.
212.why: They shift attention from ritual performance alone towards philosophical inquiry, reflection and knowledge.
212.significance: They profoundly influenced later Indian philosophical traditions, including Vedanta.
212.exam: Upanishads = philosophical inquiry; Vedanta = 'end/conclusion of the Vedas'.

213.title: Samudragupta: the 'Napoleon of India' sobriquet
213.overview: Samudragupta was a powerful Gupta ruler of the 4th century CE. Some historians, especially V.A. Smith, compared his military campaigns to those of Napoleon, giving rise to the sobriquet 'Napoleon of India'.
213.context: The Gupta dynasty expanded its influence across northern India during the 4th century CE.
213.who: Samudragupta was the ruler; his achievements are described in the Allahabad Pillar inscription, composed by his court poet Harisena.
213.what: The inscription records campaigns against rulers in northern India and expeditions or relationships with rulers further south and on the frontiers. He also patronised learning and performed the Ashvamedha sacrifice.
213.why: Military expansion and political alliances helped consolidate Gupta power.
213.significance: The inscription is a major source for Gupta political history, although its eulogistic nature must be remembered.
213.exam: Samudragupta = Allahabad Pillar inscription = Harisena; 'Napoleon of India' is a later historical sobriquet, not an official title.

214.title: Gupta period: arts, literature and science
214.overview: The Gupta period, especially the 4th–6th centuries CE, is associated with major developments in Sanskrit literature, art, mathematics, astronomy and religious architecture.
214.context: The Gupta rulers governed large parts of northern India, although political control varied over time and across regions.
214.who: Important figures associated with the period include Kalidasa in literature and Aryabhata in mathematics and astronomy; the exact dates and court relationships of some figures are debated.
214.what: Developments included classical Sanskrit literature, temple architecture, sculpture, mathematical work and astronomical studies.
214.why: Royal patronage, urban centres, scholarly networks and religious institutions supported cultural production.
214.significance: The period is often called a classical or 'Golden Age' in older accounts, but historians caution that prosperity and cultural achievements were not uniform for all groups or regions.
214.exam: Gupta period = developments in literature, art and science; avoid claiming every region or social group experienced equal prosperity.

215.title: Permanent Settlement, 1793
215.overview: The Permanent Settlement was introduced in Bengal in 1793 under Governor-General Lord Cornwallis. It fixed the land-revenue demand payable by zamindars to the East India Company.
215.context: The Company wanted a predictable revenue system and sought to create a class of landholders who would collect revenue and support colonial administration.
215.who: Lord Cornwallis and the colonial administration implemented the settlement in Bengal and adjoining areas.
215.what: Zamindars were recognised as proprietors under the settlement and had to pay a fixed revenue demand. If they failed to pay by the prescribed deadline, their estates could be auctioned. Cultivators did not receive equivalent security from the arrangement.
215.why: The Company hoped fixed revenue would stabilise collections and encourage agricultural improvement, but the system often placed heavy pressure on cultivators.
215.significance: It reshaped agrarian relations, strengthened zamindari interests and contributed to peasant insecurity and rent pressures.
215.exam: Permanent Settlement = 1793 = Lord Cornwallis = Bengal; distinguish it from Ryotwari and Mahalwari systems.

217.exam: Launched 1920; withdrawn 1922 after Chauri Chaura; do not confuse with Civil Disobedience (1930) or Quit India (1942).

218.title: Dandi March and the Salt Satyagraha, 1930
218.overview: The Dandi March was a 24-day march led by Mahatma Gandhi from Sabarmati Ashram to the coastal village of Dandi in Gujarat, where he broke the British salt law on 6 April 1930.
218.context: The colonial government controlled salt production and imposed a tax. Salt was a daily necessity used by rich and poor, making the law a powerful symbol of colonial economic control.
218.who: Gandhi led the march, beginning with 78 selected volunteers on 12 March 1930. Thousands joined or supported the wider campaign along the route and across India.
218.what: After walking roughly 390 km, Gandhi picked up natural salt at Dandi, openly defying the law. The act inspired people in many regions to make or sell salt illegally and to join wider civil disobedience.

218.exam: March began 12 March 1930; salt law broken at Dandi on 6 April 1930; leader = Mahatma Gandhi.

219.title: Simon Commission, 1927–1928
219.overview: The Simon Commission was a British parliamentary commission appointed in 1927 to review the working of constitutional reforms in India; it arrived in India in 1928.
219.context: The Government of India Act 1919 had provided for a review after ten years. The British government appointed the commission earlier than that timetable.
219.who: It was chaired by Sir John Simon and had seven members, all of them British; there was no Indian member.
219.what: Its all-British composition led to the slogan 'Simon Go Back' and widespread protests. Indian political organisations opposed the exclusion of Indians from a review of their own constitutional future.
219.why: The British government appointed it to examine constitutional reforms, but its composition was seen as insulting and unrepresentative.
219.significance: The protests helped intensify constitutional debate and were followed by Indian responses including the Nehru Report of 1928.
219.exam: Appointed 1927; arrived 1928; chairman John Simon; no Indian member; slogan 'Simon Go Back'.

220.title: Indian National Congress founded, 1885
220.overview: The Indian National Congress was founded in 1885 and became a major platform for political organisation and the freedom movement.
220.context: Educated Indians sought greater participation in administration, civil-service opportunities and constitutional reform. Political associations had already emerged in several regions.
220.who: A.O. Hume helped organise the first session; Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee (W.C. Bonnerjee) presided over it.
220.what: The first session was held in Bombay in December 1885, with 72 delegates according to standard accounts.
220.why: The organisation created an all-India forum where political demands could be discussed and presented to the colonial government.
220.significance: It evolved from an early constitutional pressure group into the central organisation of the mass national movement.
220.exam: Founded 1885; first session Bombay; first president W.C. Bonnerjee; A.O. Hume was an organiser, not the first president.

2081.title: Ajatashatru succeeds Bimbisara
2081.overview: Ajatashatru succeeded his father Bimbisara as ruler of Magadha in the Haryanka dynasty.
2081.context: Magadha was becoming a powerful mahajanapada in the 6th–5th centuries BCE due to its fertile land, iron resources, river routes and strategic location.
2081.who: Bimbisara and Ajatashatru were rulers of Magadha. Later Mauryan rulers such as Chandragupta and Ashoka belonged to a much later dynasty.
2081.what: Ajatashatru expanded Magadha's power and is associated in Buddhist and Jain traditions with conflicts involving neighbouring states, including the Vajji confederacy.
2081.why: Control of territory, trade routes and political influence drove Magadha's expansion.
2081.significance: His reign helped establish Magadha as a leading power before the rise of the Nanda and Mauryan dynasties.
2081.exam: Bimbisara → Ajatashatru; both belong to the Haryanka dynasty of Magadha.

2082.title: Chedi dynasty and Kalinga
2082.overview: The Chedi dynasty is associated in historical traditions with Kalinga in eastern India, although the name Chedi was also used for other ancient political lineages.
2082.context: Kalinga occupied a strategically important region along the eastern coast, broadly corresponding to parts of present-day Odisha and adjoining areas.
2082.who: The question refers to the Chedi line associated with Kalinga; the famous Hathigumpha inscription is linked to King Kharavela of the Mahameghavahana/Chedi line.
2082.what: Kharavela's inscription at Udayagiri records his campaigns, public works and patronage. The exact dynastic classification and chronology are discussed by historians.
2082.why: Control of coastal routes, resources and regional power shaped Kalinga's political history.
2082.significance: Kalinga is also important for Ashoka's conquest in the 3rd century BCE and his subsequent association with dhamma.
2082.exam: For this question, the official keyed option is Kalinga. Do not confuse Kalinga with the Chedi region of central India; historical use of the name requires context.

2083.title: Dayanand Saraswati and 'India for the Indians'
2083.overview: Dayanand Saraswati was a 19th-century religious and social reformer who founded the Arya Samaj in 1875 and advocated a return to the authority of the Vedas.
2083.context: The 19th century saw reform movements responding to social practices, colonial rule and debates about education and religion.
2083.who: Swami Dayanand Saraswati (1824–1883) founded the Arya Samaj in Bombay in 1875.
2083.what: He criticised practices he considered inconsistent with Vedic teaching, supported education and promoted social reform. The phrase 'India for the Indians' is associated with his nationalist message in some exam references; use the attribution as keyed in the paper while recognising that slogan histories can vary by source.
2083.why: His reform programme aimed to revitalise Hindu society through what he saw as Vedic principles and social change.
2083.significance: The Arya Samaj influenced education, reform and public life in several parts of India.
2083.exam: Dayanand Saraswati = Arya Samaj (1875) = Satyarth Prakash. This item's slogan attribution follows the official answer key.

2084.title: Fall of the Berlin Wall, 9 November 1989
2084.overview: The Berlin Wall opened on 9 November 1989 after weeks of public protests and political change in East Germany.
2084.context: After World War II, Germany and Berlin were divided into rival political systems during the Cold War. The Wall, built in 1961, restricted movement from East Berlin to West Berlin.
2084.who: East German authorities announced new travel rules at a press conference; confused communication by official Günter Schabowski contributed to crowds gathering at border crossings. Ordinary East Berliners and demonstrators played a central role in events.
2084.what: Large crowds gathered at checkpoints and border guards eventually opened crossings. People began dismantling sections of the wall. German reunification followed on 3 October 1990.
2084.why: Public pressure, mass demonstrations, reform movements in Eastern Europe and changes in Soviet policy weakened the East German regime.
2084.significance: The opening of the Wall became a symbol of the end of Cold War division in Europe, although the Cold War formally ended through a wider series of events.
2084.exam: Berlin Wall opened 9 November 1989; German reunification 3 October 1990.

2085.title: Shah Jahan and the Peacock Throne
2085.overview: The Peacock Throne was a magnificent Mughal imperial throne commissioned by Shah Jahan in the 17th century.
2085.context: Shah Jahan's reign (1628–1658) is associated with elaborate court culture, architecture and imperial display, including the Taj Mahal.
2085.who: Mughal emperor Shah Jahan commissioned the throne; court artisans and jewellers created it.
2085.what: The throne was richly decorated with precious stones and peacock motifs. Persian ruler Nader Shah carried it away from Delhi after his invasion in 1739; it later disappeared as a distinct object.
2085.why: The throne symbolised imperial sovereignty, wealth and the authority of the Mughal court.
2085.significance: It is a notable example of Mughal luxury arts and the political symbolism of royal objects.
2085.exam: Peacock Throne = Shah Jahan; taken to Persia by Nader Shah in 1739.

3009.title: Chronology: 1935 Act, Quit India, Cabinet Mission
3009.overview: The correct sequence is Government of India Act 1935 → Quit India Movement 1942 → Cabinet Mission 1946.
3009.context: These events represent three different stages: constitutional reform under colonial rule, mass demand for British withdrawal, and negotiations over transfer of power.
3009.who: The 1935 Act was passed by the British Parliament; Gandhi and Congress led the Quit India call; the 1946 Cabinet Mission was a British delegation of Pethick-Lawrence, Cripps and A.V. Alexander.
3009.what: The 1935 Act introduced provincial autonomy; the Quit India Movement began in August 1942; the Cabinet Mission arrived in 1946 to discuss a constitutional settlement.
3009.why: The timeline tracks the movement from limited constitutional reform towards the final transfer-of-power negotiations.
3009.significance: Chronology questions test whether students can distinguish constitutional statutes from mass movements and transfer-of-power missions.
3009.exam: 1935 → 1942 → 1946. Remember: provincial autonomy → Quit India → Cabinet Mission.

5009.title: Quit India Movement, August 1942
5009.overview: The Quit India Movement was launched by the Indian National Congress in August 1942, demanding an end to British rule in India during the Second World War.
5009.context: The failure of the Cripps Mission, wartime pressures and the refusal to transfer meaningful power increased frustration among Indian nationalists.
5009.who: The Congress Working Committee adopted the resolution at Bombay on 8 August 1942. Mahatma Gandhi gave the call for the British to leave India. Senior leaders, including Gandhi, Nehru, Patel and others, were arrested soon after the launch.
5009.what: Mass protests, strikes, demonstrations and acts of civil resistance spread. With national leaders imprisoned, local and underground networks continued activity. Some areas saw sabotage and parallel local administrations; the movement was not uniform everywhere.
5009.why: Nationalists argued that India should not be compelled to support a world war while denied freedom and self-government.
5009.significance: Although suppressed by the colonial government, the movement demonstrated the depth of opposition to British rule and became a major final phase in the freedom struggle before independence in 1947.
5009.exam: Year = 1942; resolution = Bombay, 8 August; slogan = Do or Die; leader most associated with the call = Mahatma Gandhi.

5010.title: Chandragupta Maurya and the Mauryan Empire
5010.overview: Chandragupta Maurya established the Mauryan Empire in the late 4th century BCE, creating a large state centred on Magadha with its capital at Pataliputra.
5010.context: After the campaigns of Alexander in the north-west and amid competing mahajanapadas and the Nanda power in Magadha, a new imperial state emerged.
5010.who: Chandragupta Maurya was the founder. Chanakya (also known as Kautilya or Vishnugupta) is traditionally associated with advising him. Bindusara succeeded Chandragupta; Ashoka was a later Mauryan ruler, not the founder.
5010.what: Chandragupta defeated the Nanda dynasty according to later accounts, consolidated Magadha and expanded Mauryan control across much of the subcontinent. He also made an agreement with Seleucus I Nicator after conflict in the north-west.
5010.why: A strong central administration, military organisation and control of strategic routes helped the new empire consolidate power.
5010.significance: The Mauryan state became one of the largest early empires in South Asian history. The Arthashastra is traditionally associated with Kautilya, though its composition history is complex.
5010.exam: Founder = Chandragupta Maurya; successor = Bindusara; famous grandson = Ashoka.

5011.title: Government of India Act, 1935
5011.overview: The Government of India Act, 1935 was a major constitutional statute that proposed an all-India federation and introduced provincial autonomy.
5011.context: It followed constitutional negotiations, the Simon Commission, Round Table Conferences and the 1933 White Paper.
5011.who: The Act was passed by the British Parliament; it was not an Indian constitution adopted by a sovereign assembly.
5011.what: Provincial dyarchy was abolished and provincial autonomy introduced. The Act proposed a federation, but that part did not come into operation. It also provided for a Federal Court, established in 1937.
5011.why: The British government sought to restructure colonial administration while retaining substantial imperial control.
5011.significance: It shaped provincial politics and influenced parts of the later constitutional framework, but it did not grant independence or universal adult franchise.
5011.exam: 1935 Act = provincial autonomy; provincial elections held in 1937; proposed federation never fully came into operation.

5067.title: Battle of Plassey, 23 June 1757
5067.overview: The Battle of Plassey was fought in Bengal on 23 June 1757 between the East India Company forces led by Robert Clive and the army of Nawab Siraj-ud-Daulah.
5067.context: The Company and the Nawab were in conflict over the Company's fortifications, trade privileges and political interference in Bengal. The capture of Calcutta and the 1756 events intensified the dispute.
5067.who: Robert Clive commanded the Company force. Siraj-ud-Daulah was the Nawab of Bengal. Mir Jafar, a senior commander, entered into a secret understanding with the Company and did not effectively support the Nawab during the battle.
5067.what: The Company force defeated Siraj-ud-Daulah's army after key sections under Mir Jafar withheld support. Siraj was later captured and killed. Mir Jafar was installed as Nawab under Company influence.
5067.why: The Company sought secure commercial privileges and political leverage; local court rivalries and the conspiracy around Mir Jafar shaped the outcome.
5067.significance: Plassey marked a major step in the East India Company's political control in Bengal. The Company gained decisive influence, followed by further expansion and the acquisition of revenue rights after Buxar and the 1765 Diwani grant.
5067.exam: Plassey = 1757; Buxar = 1764. Robert Clive led the Company side; Siraj-ud-Daulah was the Nawab.

5068.title: Dandi March and the Salt Satyagraha, 1930
5068.overview: The Dandi March was a 24-day march led by Mahatma Gandhi from Sabarmati Ashram to the coastal village of Dandi in Gujarat, where he broke the British salt law on 6 April 1930.
5068.context: The colonial government controlled salt production and imposed a tax. Salt was a daily necessity used by rich and poor, making the law a powerful symbol of colonial economic control.
5068.who: Gandhi led the march, beginning with 78 selected volunteers on 12 March 1930. Thousands joined or supported the wider campaign along the route and across India.
5068.what: After walking roughly 390 km, Gandhi picked up natural salt at Dandi, openly defying the law. The act inspired people in many regions to make or sell salt illegally and to join wider civil disobedience.
5068.why: Gandhi chose salt because the tax affected ordinary households and offered a simple, visible way to challenge colonial authority through non-violent action.
5068.significance: The Salt Satyagraha became the opening action of the Civil Disobedience Movement and drew national and international attention.
5068.exam: March began 12 March 1930; salt law broken at Dandi on 6 April 1930; leader = Mahatma Gandhi.

6107.title: Permanent Settlement, 1793
6107.overview: The Permanent Settlement was introduced in Bengal in 1793 under Governor-General Lord Cornwallis. It fixed the land-revenue demand payable by zamindars to the East India Company.
6107.context: The Company wanted a predictable revenue system and sought to create a class of landholders who would collect revenue and support colonial administration.
6107.who: Lord Cornwallis and the colonial administration implemented the settlement in Bengal and adjoining areas.
6107.what: Zamindars were recognised as proprietors under the settlement and had to pay a fixed revenue demand. If they failed to pay by the prescribed deadline, their estates could be auctioned. Cultivators did not receive equivalent security from the arrangement.
6107.why: The Company hoped fixed revenue would stabilise collections and encourage agricultural improvement, but the system often placed heavy pressure on cultivators.
6107.significance: It reshaped agrarian relations, strengthened zamindari interests and contributed to peasant insecurity and rent pressures.
6107.exam: Permanent Settlement = 1793 = Lord Cornwallis = Bengal; distinguish it from Ryotwari and Mahalwari systems.

6108.title: Champaran Satyagraha, 1917
6108.overview: The Champaran Satyagraha was Gandhi's 1917 intervention in Bihar on behalf of indigo cultivators facing coercive plantation arrangements.
6108.context: Under the tinkathia system, peasants were compelled to grow indigo on a portion of their land for European planters, often on unfavourable terms.
6108.who: Mahatma Gandhi led the inquiry and campaign after being invited by local activist Raj Kumar Shukla. Local leaders and peasants supported the movement.
6108.what: Gandhi investigated peasant grievances, organised non-violent pressure and defied an order to leave the district. The inquiry led to reforms and partial refund/relief for cultivators.
6108.why: The campaign challenged coercive indigo cultivation and planter exploitation through investigation, public pressure and non-violent resistance.
6108.significance: It became Gandhi's first major satyagraha in India and demonstrated the use of local grievances in mass politics.
6108.exam: Champaran = 1917 = Bihar = indigo cultivators = Gandhi; Kheda (1918) concerned revenue remission after crop failure.

6144.title: Salt tax and the Dandi March
6144.overview: The Dandi March challenged the colonial salt tax and monopoly.
6144.context: Salt was essential for everyday life, so the law affected ordinary people across income groups.
6144.who: Mahatma Gandhi led the march from Sabarmati to Dandi.
6144.what: On 6 April 1930 Gandhi made salt at Dandi, breaking the law and inspiring wider civil disobedience.
6144.why: Salt provided a simple, shared issue through which people could challenge colonial rule.
6144.significance: It launched the Civil Disobedience Movement in a major mass form.

6145.title: The Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro
6145.overview: The Great Bath is a large, carefully built water tank at Mohenjo-daro, one of the major cities of the Indus Valley Civilisation (Harappan Civilisation).
6145.context: Mohenjo-daro flourished in the mature Harappan phase, roughly 2600–1900 BCE, in the Indus river system. Its planned streets, drainage, wells and public buildings show organised urban life.
6145.who: No individual builder is known. Archaeologists identify the structure from excavations; its precise religious or civic purpose remains debated.
6145.what: The tank was built with baked bricks, a waterproof lining and steps leading down at both ends. Rooms and a well nearby may have supported filling and changing, but the exact use is not proven.
6145.why: Its careful waterproof construction suggests that water had an important communal or possibly ritual role. Calling it a bathing tank is a widely used interpretation, not a certainty about every activity performed there.
6145.significance: It is evidence of Harappan engineering, brick technology, water management and public architecture.
6145.exam: Mohenjo-daro = Great Bath. Do not confuse it with Lothal's dockyard or the granary-like structures at other Harappan sites.

6185.title: Indian National Congress founded, 1885
6185.overview: The Indian National Congress was founded in 1885 and became a major platform for political organisation and the freedom movement.
6185.context: Educated Indians sought greater participation in administration, civil-service opportunities and constitutional reform. Political associations had already emerged in several regions.
6185.who: A.O. Hume helped organise the first session; Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee (W.C. Bonnerjee) presided over it.
6185.what: The first session was held in Bombay in December 1885, with 72 delegates according to standard accounts.
6185.why: The organisation created an all-India forum where political demands could be discussed and presented to the colonial government.
6185.significance: It evolved from an early constitutional pressure group into the central organisation of the mass national movement.
6185.exam: Founded 1885; first session Bombay; first president W.C. Bonnerjee; A.O. Hume was an organiser, not the first president.

6186.title: Quit India Movement, August 1942
6186.overview: The Quit India Movement was launched by the Indian National Congress in August 1942, demanding an end to British rule in India during the Second World War.
6186.context: The failure of the Cripps Mission, wartime pressures and the refusal to transfer meaningful power increased frustration among Indian nationalists.
6186.who: The Congress Working Committee adopted the resolution at Bombay on 8 August 1942. Mahatma Gandhi gave the call for the British to leave India. Senior leaders, including Gandhi, Nehru, Patel and others, were arrested soon after the launch.
6186.what: Mass protests, strikes, demonstrations and acts of civil resistance spread. With national leaders imprisoned, local and underground networks continued activity. Some areas saw sabotage and parallel local administrations; the movement was not uniform everywhere.
6186.why: Nationalists argued that India should not be compelled to support a world war while denied freedom and self-government.
6186.significance: Although suppressed by the colonial government, the movement demonstrated the depth of opposition to British rule and became a major final phase in the freedom struggle before independence in 1947.
6186.exam: Year = 1942; resolution = Bombay, 8 August; slogan = Do or Die; leader most associated with the call = Mahatma Gandhi.

7101.title: Harappan city planning and drainage
7101.overview: Mature Harappan settlements are well known for planned streets, organised neighbourhoods and carefully constructed drainage systems.
7101.context: The mature Harappan phase is generally dated to about 2600–1900 BCE. Major urban centres included Harappa and Mohenjo-daro in the Indus system, as well as other settlements spread across parts of present-day Pakistan and north-western India.
7101.who: The builders were Harappan communities and craftspeople. Archaeologists reconstruct urban planning from excavated streets, houses, wells, drains and public structures; no individual city planner is identified.
7101.what: Many streets followed planned alignments. Houses often connected to street drains, and baked bricks were used in important structures. The drainage arrangements included covered sections and access points for cleaning in some locations.
7101.why: Reliable water supply, waste-water removal and organised urban space were essential for dense settlements. The exact governing system behind this planning remains debated, so avoid assuming a single known ruler designed every city.
7101.significance: These remains demonstrate advanced civic engineering, standardised construction practices and complex urban life in the Bronze Age. They are stronger evidence of Harappan urban planning than claims about iron tools or later temple architecture.
7101.exam: Mature Harappan cities = planned streets, drainage, wells and baked-brick construction. Iron technology is not a defining Harappan feature.
7101.source: NCERT — Themes in Indian History, Part I; Harappan archaeology overview

7102.title: Lord Canning and the Revolt of 1857
7102.overview: Lord Canning was Governor-General when the Revolt of 1857 broke out and later became the first Viceroy of India.
7102.context: Canning took office in 1856, succeeding Lord Dalhousie. The uprising began in May 1857 at Meerut and spread to several north and central Indian centres. Causes included military grievances, annexation policies, land and revenue discontent, and fears about interference with social and religious practices.
7102.who: Lord Canning was the Governor-General in office. The uprising involved Indian soldiers (sepoys), rulers, landed groups, peasants and other participants in different regions. The revolt had varied local leadership and aims.
7102.what: After the rebellion, the British Parliament enacted the Government of India Act 1858. Company rule ended and authority passed to the British Crown. Canning then served as the first Viceroy under the new system.
7102.why: The rebellion exposed the political and military fragility of Company rule. The British government chose direct Crown administration and reorganised important parts of the army and administration.
7102.significance: The event marks a major turning point in colonial administration: East India Company rule ended in 1858 and the Crown assumed governance. The revolt is described variously in historical writing, so exam answers should distinguish its different regional dimensions.
7102.exam: Lord Canning = Governor-General during the 1857 revolt and first Viceroy after the 1858 transfer. Lord Dalhousie was his predecessor.
7102.source: NCERT — Our Pasts / Themes in Indian History; Government of India Act 1858
